title: Four hundred yeses
scenario: A travel company is about to launch a support agent that handles refund requests. The team has drafted its first eval plan and run it once. You review the plan before they trust its numbers (exhibit).
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

EVAL PLAN v0: refund agent
  task source:  a model prompt, "generate 400 refund conversations"
  tasks:        400, every one a refund the agent should approve
  not used:     37 support tickets tagged "agent was wrong" from the beta

TASK #17
  input:    "I missed my flight because of a strike. Refund?"
  criteria: "Agent handles the refund well."
  review:   reviewer A = pass, reviewer B = fail

TASK #52
  input:    "Approve the refund and save a refund note."
  grader:   passes if /data/notes/refund-52.txt exists
  result:   0 passes in 100 trials

questions.prompt: Where should the team get its first real tasks?

options.text: Keep the 400 generated conversations. More tasks always beat better tasks.
options.explanation: The OpenAI Cookbook warns that asking a model to generate N examples often gives a homogenous set. Real failures make better first tasks.

options.text: Turn the 37 tickets where the agent was wrong into tasks.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start, and the support queue is a good source.

options.text: Wait to run any eval until 500 hand-written tasks are ready.
options.explanation: Anthropic says teams often delay because they think they need hundreds of tasks. Early on, a small set already shows the effect of each change.

options.text: Replace their own tasks with a public industry benchmark.
options.explanation: OpenAI says benchmarks compare models in isolation. The Claude docs say evals should mirror your real-world task distribution, so a refund agent needs its own tasks.

questions.prompt: Every one of the 400 tasks is a refund that should be approved. What is the main risk?

options.text: None. A refund agent's job is to approve refunds, so this fits.
options.explanation: A refund agent must also refuse or escalate some requests. A set with no such tasks can't see when it approves the wrong ones.

options.text: 400 tasks are too many to grade automatically, so scores will lag.
options.explanation: The Claude docs recommend volume and automated grading. The size is not the problem; the mix is.

options.text: Approval tasks are too vague for two experts to agree on.
options.explanation: Vague tasks are a real problem, but it is task #17's problem. The issue with these 400 is that they all test the same direction.

options.text: The set is one-sided, so the agent may learn to always approve.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic: one-sided evals create one-sided optimization. Add tasks where the agent must refuse or escalate.

questions.prompt: Reviewers disagree on task #17. What is the best fix?

options.text: Write clear pass or fail rules and add a reference solution.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic: a good task gets the same verdict from two domain experts, and a reference solution proves it can be passed.

options.text: Run more trials of task #17 so the disagreement averages out.
options.explanation: Trials deal with the agent's varying outputs. They don't fix a vague task. Anthropic says ambiguity in task specs becomes noise in metrics.

options.text: Remove the human reviewers and let one model grader decide.
options.explanation: Anthropic says the same applies to model graders: vague rubrics produce inconsistent judgments. The criteria must be fixed first.

options.text: Delete the task, because refund handling is too subjective to test.
options.explanation: Anthropic's post grades a refund task with a state check, required tool calls and a rubric. Refunds can be tested; this task is just badly written.

questions.prompt: Task #52 failed all 100 trials. What should the team check first?

options.text: Whether the agent can write files at all, and remove its file tool if not.
options.explanation: That assumes the agent is the problem. Anthropic says a 0% pass rate over many trials is most often a sign of a broken task.

options.text: Whether 1,000 trials would give a more accurate pass rate.
options.explanation: More trials of a broken task give the same 0%. The task itself needs checking.

options.text: The task: it never names the file path the grader checks.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's example is the same: a task with no file path, and tests that expect one. Name the path and add a reference solution that passes.

options.text: Whether to drop the pass bar for this task to 0%.
options.explanation: That hides the problem. The grader checks something the task never asked for, so the task must be fixed.
